stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
passage:
The following text is from an original short story.
Marisol had expected the abandoned greenhouse to be empty, but it was ______ with life: ferns crowded every bench, and vines had climbed all the way to the cracked glass roof.

choices.text: teeming
devoid
reminiscent
wary

hints: What do the details after the colon show about the greenhouse?
Predict a word meaning 'full of' before reading the choices.
teaching_explanation: The colon introduces evidence that the greenhouse was full of plants. "Teeming with life" means crowded with living things, which matches ferns on every bench and vines up to the roof.
strategy_explanation: Predict "full," then choose the closest precise word.
remember: Let the text's evidence choose the word.

distractors.rationale: "Devoid" means completely lacking, the opposite of what the details describe.
"Reminiscent" means suggestive of something else and is followed by "of," not "with"; it does not describe abundance.
"Wary" means cautious, a quality of people or animals, not of a greenhouse.

strategies.explanation: Predict "full," then choose the closest precise word.

stem: Which choice best describes the function of the quotation in the text as a whole?
passage: Bridges are usually admired for their spans, the distances between their supports. Engineer Tomás Reyes, however, argues that the most important part of a bridge is the part no one sees: its foundation. "A long span on a weak foundation," he says, "is simply a dramatic way to fail."

choices.text: It presents a counterargument that Reyes goes on to reject.
It explains how engineers measure the span of a bridge.
It illustrates, in memorable terms, why Reyes believes a bridge's foundation matters more than its span.
It suggests that most existing bridges were built on weak foundations.

hints: What is Reyes's main claim?
How does the quotation relate to that claim?
teaching_explanation: Reyes claims the foundation is the most important part of a bridge. The quotation backs that claim with a vivid image: however impressive the span, a weak foundation means failure.
strategy_explanation: Identify the claim first, then ask how the quotation serves it.
remember: Function questions ask what a part does for the whole.

distractors.rationale: The quotation is Reyes's own statement supporting his view, not a counterargument.
The quotation says nothing about how spans are measured.
The quotation describes a hypothetical case and makes no claim about most existing bridges.

strategies.explanation: Identify the claim first, then ask how the quotation serves it.

stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
passage: Once a month, a community center in the town of Alder Creek hosts a "repair café," where volunteers fix residents' broken lamps, toasters, and bicycles for free. Organizers say the event keeps hundreds of items out of the landfill each year. Just as important, they add, residents who watch the repairs often learn to fix similar problems on their own.

choices.text: The repair café in Alder Creek mainly repairs bicycles.
A monthly event in Alder Creek reduces waste and helps residents learn to fix things themselves.
Volunteers in Alder Creek are paid to repair residents' household items.
Residents of Alder Creek throw away fewer items than residents of other towns do.

hints: What is the whole text about?
Which choice includes both benefits the organizers mention?
teaching_explanation: The text describes the repair café and its two benefits: keeping items out of the landfill and teaching residents repair skills. B captures both.
strategy_explanation: Summarize in one sentence, then match.
remember: The main idea covers the whole text, not one example.

distractors.rationale: Bicycles are one example among several; the text does not say they are the main focus.
The repairs are done for free by volunteers; nothing says the volunteers are paid.
The text makes no comparison with other towns.

strategies.explanation: Summarize in one sentence, then match.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's conclusion?
passage:
A student counted the birds visiting three feeders in her yard over four weeks. Each feeder held a different food.
Feeder | Food | Total visits
1 | Sunflower seeds | 212
2 | Thistle seeds | 87
3 | Suet | 145
The student concluded that, of the three foods, sunflower seeds attracted the most visits.

choices.text: Feeder 1, which held sunflower seeds, had 212 visits, more than either the thistle feeder (87) or the suet feeder (145).
Feeder 2, which held thistle seeds, had 87 visits, fewer than Feeder 3.
Together, the three feeders received 444 visits.
Feeder 3, which held suet, had 145 visits.

hints: What exactly does the conclusion claim?
Which choice compares sunflower seeds with both other foods?
teaching_explanation: The conclusion is that sunflower seeds attracted the most visits. Supporting it requires comparing the sunflower feeder with both others: 212 is greater than 87 and 145. Only A makes that full comparison.
strategy_explanation: Restate the claim, then choose the data that compares all three.
remember: A 'most' claim needs a comparison with every other option.

distractors.rationale: This compares only the other two feeders and says nothing about sunflower seeds.
The total does not show which food attracted the most visits.
One feeder's count alone cannot show which food was most popular.

strategies.explanation: Restate the claim, then choose the data that compares all three.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: The town's first canal opened in ______ within ten years, the number of businesses along its route had tripled.

choices.text: 1825, which

hints: Is each part of the sentence a complete sentence on its own?
What punctuation can join two complete sentences without a conjunction?
teaching_explanation: "The town's first canal opened in 1825" and "within ten years, the number of businesses along its route had tripled" are both independent clauses. A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses.
strategy_explanation: Two independent clauses with no conjunction need a semicolon or a period.
remember: Semicolon: two complete sentences, no conjunction.

distractors.rationale: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.
With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.
"Which" makes the second part a relative clause, but the rest of the sentence ("within ten years, the number … had tripled") cannot follow "which" grammatically.

strategies.explanation: Two independent clauses with no conjunction need a semicolon or a period.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: The collection of letters, which spans four decades and includes notes from dozens of correspondents, ______ historians a rare view of daily life in the port city.

choices.text: offer
have offered
offers
are offering

hints: Cross out the phrase and clause that describe the subject.
Is "collection" singular or plural?
teaching_explanation: The subject is "collection," which is singular; "of letters" and the clause between commas are modifiers. The singular verb "offers" agrees, and the clause's own verbs ("spans," "includes") confirm the singular subject.
strategy_explanation: Strip it down to "The collection … ______ historians a rare view"; only the singular verb fits.
remember: Find the true subject, then match the verb.

distractors.rationale: "Offer" is plural, agreeing with "letters" or "correspondents" rather than the subject "collection."
"Have offered" is plural.
"Are offering" is plural.

strategies.explanation: Strip it down to "The collection … ______ historians a rare view"; only the singular verb fits.

stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
passage: Most frogs lay their eggs in water, where the young hatch as swimming tadpoles. The coquí frogs of Puerto Rico, ______ lay their eggs on land, and the young hatch as tiny, fully formed frogs.

choices.text: for example,
therefore,
however,
similarly,

hints: Is the coquí like most frogs or different from them?
Choose the transition that signals that relationship.
teaching_explanation: The first sentence describes most frogs; the second describes coquí frogs doing the opposite (eggs on land, no tadpoles). "However" signals that contrast.
strategy_explanation: Predict a contrast word such as 'but,' then match.
remember: Name the relationship before choosing the transition.

distractors.rationale: Coquí frogs are an exception to the pattern, not an example of it.
The coquí's behavior is not a result of what most frogs do.
"Similarly" signals likeness, but the coquí differs from most frogs.

strategies.explanation: Predict a contrast word such as 'but,' then match.

stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between recycling glass and recycling plastic. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Glass bottles and plastic bottles can both be recycled.
• Glass can be recycled again and again without losing quality.
• Most plastics can be recycled only a few times before the material degrades.
• Recycled glass is often used to make new bottles.

choices.text: Glass bottles and plastic bottles can both be recycled.
Recycled glass is often used to make new bottles.
Both glass and plastic are commonly used to make bottles, and both can be recycled.
Glass can be recycled again and again without losing quality, whereas most plastics can be recycled only a few times before the material degrades.

hints: The goal is to emphasize a difference.
Which choice mentions both materials and contrasts them?
teaching_explanation: The goal is a difference. D contrasts how many times each material can be recycled, using "whereas" to make the difference explicit.
strategy_explanation: Underline the goal (difference), then eliminate choices that state similarities or mention one material.
remember: Synthesis questions: the stated goal decides the answer.

distractors.rationale: This states a similarity, not a difference.
This gives information about glass only, with no comparison to plastic.
This states similarities between the materials.

strategies.explanation: Underline the goal (difference), then eliminate choices that state similarities or mention one material.

stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
passage: For years, many biologists assumed that tardigrades, tiny animals that can survive being almost completely dried out, protected themselves mainly by producing a sugar called trehalose, which helps shield cells in some other organisms. Yet when researchers measured trehalose in several tardigrade species, they found little or none. Further work identified proteins found only in tardigrades that form a glass-like gel as the animals dry, apparently protecting their cells until water returns.

choices.text: It presents two competing explanations and concludes that neither is supported.
It describes an experiment and then lists that experiment's limitations.
It describes a long-held assumption, presents evidence against it, and then reports an alternative explanation.
It introduces an animal and compares it with other organisms that produce trehalose.

hints: Track the text sentence by sentence: assumption, then what?
What does the last sentence offer?
teaching_explanation: The text opens with an assumption (trehalose protects tardigrades), gives evidence against it (little or no trehalose found), and ends with an alternative (tardigrade-specific proteins forming a gel).
strategy_explanation: Label each sentence's role, then match the sequence.
remember: Structure questions: label each sentence's job.

distractors.rationale: The text does reach a supported explanation: the proteins.
No limitations of an experiment are listed.
The text mentions other organisms only briefly and does not compare tardigrades with them.

strategies.explanation: Label each sentence's role, then match the sequence.

stem: Which quotation from "The Old Orchard" most effectively illustrates the claim?
passage: In an original poem titled "The Old Orchard," the speaker describes a neglected orchard as both decaying and still productive, as this line shows: ______

choices.text: "Wind has stripped the orchard to its bones."
"Each autumn the pickers fill their baskets."
"The farmhouse windows glow at dusk."
"The branches sag with rot, and still they bloom."

hints: The claim has two parts. What are they?
Which quotation shows both at once?
teaching_explanation: The claim has two parts: decaying and still productive. "The branches sag with rot" shows decay, and "still they bloom" shows continued growth. Only D shows both.
strategy_explanation: Eliminate quotations that show only one half of the claim.
remember: Two-part claims need evidence for both parts.

distractors.rationale: This shows decay only.
This shows productivity only, and it describes the pickers, not the orchard's condition.
This describes the farmhouse, not the orchard.

strategies.explanation: Eliminate quotations that show only one half of the claim.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
passage: The museum's new exhibit focuses on three everyday objects whose inventors are largely forgotten ______ the folding ladder, the safety pin, and the paper clip.

choices.text: forgotten:
forgotten;
forgotten, which
forgotten and

hints: Is the part before the blank a complete sentence?
What punctuation introduces a list that explains what came before?
teaching_explanation: The first part is a complete sentence that announces three objects, and the list that follows names them. A colon correctly introduces a list after a complete clause.
strategy_explanation: A complete clause followed by a list calls for a colon.
remember: Use a colon after a complete clause to introduce a list.

distractors.rationale: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the list is not a clause.
"Which" cannot introduce a list of nouns without a verb.
"And" joins the list to the clause ungrammatically, leaving no verb for the list.

strategies.explanation: A complete clause followed by a list calls for a colon.

was

Is "each" singular or plural?

distractors.rationale: "Were" agrees with "volunteers" or "booths," not the true subject "Each."

passage: Although the two ______ findings at first seemed to contradict each other, a closer look showed that they had measured the lake's temperature at different depths.

choices.text: scientist's
scientists
scientists's
scientists'

hints: How many scientists are there?
How is a plural noun ending in s made possessive?
teaching_explanation: The findings belong to two scientists, so the plural possessive is needed. For a plural noun ending in s, add only an apostrophe: "scientists'."
remember: Plural possessive: add just an apostrophe after s.

distractors.rationale: "Scientist's" is singular possessive, but there are two scientists.
"Scientists" without an apostrophe is a plain plural, not a possessive.
"Scientists's" is not standard for a plural possessive.

passage: Some critics predicted that the redesigned riverside park would attract few visitors. ______ attendance during its first summer was double that of the previous year.

choices.text: Similarly,
Therefore,
On the contrary,
For example,

hints: Did the attendance match or contradict the prediction?
Pick the transition for that relationship.
teaching_explanation: The critics predicted few visitors; attendance instead doubled. "On the contrary" signals that the second sentence contradicts the prediction.
remember: Name the relationship, then the transition.

"Therefore" signals a result, but the prediction did not cause the attendance.

stem: The student wants to introduce Lin Adeyemi and her best-known work to an audience unfamiliar with her. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Lin Adeyemi was a twentieth-century painter.
• She painted large murals in train stations.
• Her murals depicted ordinary commuters.
• Her 1962 mural Morning Platform is her best-known work.

choices.text: Lin Adeyemi, a twentieth-century painter known for her murals of ordinary commuters in train stations, is best remembered for her 1962 mural Morning Platform.
Morning Platform is Lin Adeyemi's best-known mural.
Ordinary commuters appear in many murals painted in train stations.
In 1962, a mural called Morning Platform was painted.

hints: What does an audience unfamiliar with her need to know first?
Which choice covers both the painter and the work?
teaching_explanation: An unfamiliar audience needs to know who Adeyemi was as well as her best-known work. A identifies her as a twentieth-century muralist of commuters and names Morning Platform.
strategy_explanation: The goal has two parts: introduce her and her best-known work.
remember: Introductions identify the subject before details.

distractors.rationale: This names the work but does not tell an unfamiliar audience who Adeyemi was.
This does not mention Adeyemi or her work.
This omits the painter entirely.

strategies.explanation: The goal has two parts: introduce her and her best-known work.

stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?
passage:
Text 1
Some teachers argue that the fastest way for students to build vocabulary is to memorize lists of words and their definitions. Students can review dozens of words in a single sitting, and quiz scores often rise within days.

Text 2
Researchers who study reading point out that definitions memorized for a quiz are often forgotten within weeks. Words met repeatedly in meaningful reading, by contrast, tend to be retained, because readers see how the words are actually used.

choices.text: They would argue that quizzes are the most reliable way to measure vocabulary growth.
They would grant that memorizing lists can raise quiz scores quickly but question whether those gains last.
They would claim that students cannot learn any new words by memorizing lists.
They would suggest that reading builds vocabulary faster than memorizing lists does.

hints: Does Text 2 deny that lists raise quiz scores?
What does Text 2 say happens weeks later?
teaching_explanation: Text 1 claims lists are the fastest way to build vocabulary, citing quick quiz gains. Text 2 does not deny quick gains; it says memorized definitions are often forgotten within weeks, while words met in reading tend to stick. So the researchers would accept the short-term gains but doubt they last.
strategy_explanation: Find where Text 2 addresses memorized definitions, then pick the response that matches its partial agreement.
remember: Watch for partial agreement and extreme wording.

distractors.rationale: Text 2 implies quiz results can mislead, since memorized words fade; it does not call quizzes the most reliable measure.
Text 2 says memorized words are "often forgotten," not that students learn none; "cannot learn any" goes too far.
Text 2 argues that reading leads to better retention, not faster learning.

strategies.explanation: Find where Text 2 addresses memorized definitions, then pick the response that matches its partial agreement.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
passage: Marine biologists have observed that when an empty shell larger than any in a group appears, hermit crabs nearby often line up by size beside it. When the largest crab moves into the new shell, the next crab in line takes the shell it left behind, and so on down the line. This pattern suggests that ______

choices.text: hermit crabs generally prefer shells that are too small for them.
only the largest crab in the group ends up with a better-fitting shell.
hermit crabs line up beside a new shell without regard to their size.
a single new shell can lead to several crabs in the group moving into larger shells.

hints: Follow the chain: what happens to each shell that is left behind?
How many crabs end up in a new shell?
teaching_explanation: Each crab that moves leaves its old shell for the next crab, and the chain continues down the line. So one new shell lets many crabs upgrade, not just one.
strategy_explanation: Trace the sequence in the second sentence to its result.
remember: Completion questions follow the text's logic to its next step.

distractors.rationale: The crabs move into larger shells, which suggests they seek a better fit, not smaller shells.
The chain of moves means crabs after the largest one also get larger shells.
The text says the crabs line up by size.

strategies.explanation: Trace the sequence in the second sentence to its result.
